Seminar Title:

Development of Antimicrobial Films from Animal Byproduct–Derived Biopolymers (Gelatin/Chitosan-Lactate) for Chicken Meat Preservation

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Food Process Engineering

Speaker Name:

Rahul Thakur ( Rollno : 521fp6007)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

CH-113

Date and Time:

07 Sep 2026 5 15 PM

Contact:

Preetam Sarkar

Abstract:

The growing demand for safe, sustainable, and environmentally friendly food packaging materials has stimulated the development of biodegradable and active packaging systems derived from natural polymers. Conventional petroleum-based plastics raise significant environmental concerns owing to their non-biodegradable nature and the potential migration of harmful substances into food products. In response, biopolymeric materials obtained from renewable resources have emerged as promising alternatives. Among protein- and polysaccharide-based polymers, gelatin (G) and chitosan exhibit excellent film-forming ability, biodegradability, and compatibility with functional additives. The incorporation of natural bioactive compounds and nanostructured materials into polymer matrices further offers an effective approach to enhancing the physicochemical, antimicrobial, and barrier properties of biodegradable packaging films. Accordingly, the present study focused on developing antimicrobial and nanocomposite biopolymeric films based on gelatin (G) and chitosan-lactate (ChL), incorporating curcuma hydroethanolic extract (CEE), cellulose nanospheres (CNS), TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanospheres (TCNS), and nisin (N), and evaluating their application in the preservation of fresh chicken meat.

The rheological properties of the film-forming solutions (FFS) demonstrated that the incorporation of ChL into G significantly enhanced the dynamic moduli and apparent viscosity. The addition of CEE, CNS, and N produced a modest increase in viscosity, whereas TCNS had the least influence on viscosity. ChL enhanced the film elongation at break (EAB) to 51.51 &plusmn 2.37%, while CEE reduced it to 21.85 &plusmn 2.04%. Although ChL decreased tensile strength (TS), the incorporation of CEE and CNS improved it. TCNS further increased TS to 49.3 &plusmn 2.12 MPa, while nisin enhanced EAB to 44.55 &plusmn 1.77% from 35.14 &plusmn 1.74%. The hydrophilic nature of ChL and N increased the films&rsquo moisture content and water solubility with increasing concentration. In contrast, TCNS-based films exhibited superior structural integrity, tensile strength, thermal stability, morphology, and hydrophobicity compared with films containing untreated CNS. The incorporation of CEE further improved UV shielding, water vapour barrier performance, tensile strength, heat resistance, cross-linking, and antimicrobial activity. However, increasing CNS and TCNS concentrations reduced these parameters. Contact angle measurements, reaching 107.04 &plusmn 4.27&deg, confirmed the enhanced hydrophobicity imparted by CEE and TCNS. The presence of CEE and CNS also significantly improved water vapour and UV barrier properties. FTIR spectroscopy indicated enhanced intermolecular hydrogen bonding among G, ChL, CEE, CNS, TCNS, and N with increasing CEE and CNS concentrations. Morphological analysis revealed reduced surface roughness following the incorporation of CEE and N, whereas CNS and TCNS increased roughness. TCNS exhibited better compatibility with the film matrix than CNS. Thermal analysis confirmed improved thermal stability following the incorporation of these components. Antioxidant assays demonstrated that CEE-containing films achieved the highest antioxidant activity of 73.38 &plusmn 0.87%. Furthermore, G/ChL/CEE-based films exhibited notable antimicrobial activity at higher CEE concentrations. Shelf-life studies indicated that the developed films preserved fresh chicken meat for 10 days at 4 &plusmn 1 &degC, while the incorporation of both CEE and CNS extended preservation to 12 days. The synergistic effect of N and CEE further enhanced antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli and Bacillus cereus, with inhibition zones of 14.65 &plusmn 0.43 mm and 16.62 &plusmn 0.28 mm, respectively. Application of these films to fresh chicken meat stored at 4 &plusmn 1 &degC for up to 15 days demonstrated their potential as sustainable, multifunctional alternatives to conventional plastic packaging. Overall, this research highlights the potential of biopolymer-based films to provide sustainable and functional food packaging solutions while addressing the challenges of plastic waste and food preservation.
